summary: Describes small but non-interoperable changes to DNS request and transaction signature records, SIG(0), which experience showed were necessary. It lets requests and responses be signed with a public key.

eli5.summary: A DNS message can carry a signature to prove who sent it. This fixes small details in how that signature is made.

questions: how long is a sig(0) valid
subtitle: How a DNS message can carry a public-key signature that proves who sent a request or answered it.

tldr.problem: Secure DNS in RFC 2535 protects data records but not requests, message headers or the overall integrity of a response. Implementation experience showed the original SIG(0) rules needed fixing.
tldr.mechanism: A SIG(0) is a SIG record with a type covered field of zero, placed at the end of the additional information section. It signs the message, and for a response also the query that produced it, with a public key.
tldr.outcome: The changes are minor but not interoperable with RFC 2535. This document replaces the SIG(0) parts of RFC 2535, and its signature now also covers the inception and expiration times to resist replay.

facts.label: Time bracket
facts.value: Not more than 5 minutes past or future

today: RFC 2931 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2535, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its SIG(0) rules replace the corresponding parts of RFC 2535.

sections.title: What RFC 2931 Changes
sections.content:
This document makes minor but non-interoperable changes to part of RFC 2535, and assumes you know that RFC. It concerns SIG resource records that digitally sign DNS requests and transactions (responses). Such a record has a type covered field of zero, so it is often called a SIG(0).

The changes come from implementation and attempted implementation experience with TSIG (RFC 2845) and the RFC 2535 specification of SIG(0). The sections of RFC 2535 updated are all of 4.1.8.1 and parts of 4.2 and 4.3. Nothing changes for KEY or NXT records, or for how data origin and denial of existence are authenticated.
sections.eli5: Someone tried the old way of sealing DNS letters and found small mistakes. This paper fixes them, even though the fixed seals do not match the old ones.

sections.title: Why SIG(0) Exists
sections.content:
The regular SIG, KEY and NXT records of RFC 2535 protect data records, or prove that they do not exist. They give no protection for glue records, for DNS requests, for message headers on requests or responses, or for the overall integrity of a response. SIG(0) fills that gap.

Transaction authentication lets a requester be sure that messages come from the server it queried and answer the query it sent. This is done by optionally adding a TSIG record or a SIG(0) at the end of the response, which signs the server's response joined with the query.

Request authentication adds a TSIG or a special SIG(0) at the end of a request. It does nothing useful for servers older than dynamic update, and a few of those return errors or ignore requests with a non-empty additional information section. The syntax is defined for dynamic update requests (RFC 2136), TKEY requests (RFC 2930) and future requests needing authentication.
sections.eli5: The old seals only protected the facts inside a letter. Now the whole envelope, the question and the answer can be sealed too.

sections.title: Keys and the Difference From TSIG
sections.content:
For a response, the private key belongs to the host composing the DNS response message, not to the zone. For a request it may belong to the host or entity composing it, or to a zone to be affected, depending on what authority is being established. The matching public keys are normally stored in the DNS as KEY records with a protocol byte of 3 (DNSSEC) or 255 (ANY). Because requests and replies vary so much, the signatures cannot be pre-calculated, so the private key must be kept on-line.

TSIG uses secret keys installed at both ends and keyed hash codes that are relatively inexpensive to compute. SIG(0) uses public key authentication, which involves relatively expensive operations, and verifying one means obtaining and verifying the signer's KEY record. Signing every request and verifying before answering could, for some configurations, lead to a deadly embrace: fetching the KEY needs more signed requests, which need more KEYs, and so on.

So SIG(0)s SHOULD only be used on requests when needed to show the requester has some required privilege or identity. A SIG(0) on a reply does not need one on the request. For other replies, whether the server signs them or the requester requires signatures SHOULD be a local configuration option.
sections.eli5: Two friends with the same secret password can check each other quickly, like TSIG. A public-key seal works with strangers but takes much longer to check, so you use it only when it really matters.

sections.title: The SIG(0) Record
sections.content:
The structure and type number of SIG records are still given in RFC 2535 Section 4.1, but all of 4.1.8.1 and the SIG(0) parts of 4.2 and 4.3 are replaced by this document. Any conflict about SIG(0) is resolved in favor of RFC 2931.

For every transaction SIG(0), the signer field MUST be a name of the originating host, and a KEY record MUST exist at that name holding the matching public key. The inverse IP address mapping name of the host may be used if the KEY is stored there.

For all SIG(0)s the owner name, class, TTL and original TTL are meaningless. The TTL fields SHOULD be zero, the CLASS SHOULD be ANY, and to save space the owner name SHOULD be root (a single zero octet).

When a SIG(0) is wanted on a response, it MUST be the highest priority additional information. If it cannot be added without truncating the message, the server MUST change the response to hold only the question and the SIG(0), with the TC bit set and RCODE 0 (NOERROR). The client should then retry over TCP.
sections.eli5: The seal has a name tag saying who made it. The other label parts are not used, so they are left blank or tiny to save room.

sections.title: Calculating Request and Transaction Signatures
sections.content:
A request may be signed by putting one SIG(0) at the end of the query's additional information section. It signs the preceding message including the DNS header, but not the UDP/IP header, and before the request record counts are adjusted for the SIG(0). The signed data is the SIG(0) RDATA with the signature field omitted entirely (not zeroed), followed by the request.

A transaction signature on a response covers the SIG RDATA without the signature, the entire query message that produced the response, and the entire response message, again before the counts are adjusted. If the check succeeds, the requester knows the query and response were not tampered with in transit, that the response matches the intended query, and that it came from the queried server.

Over TCP, the first data packet is signed as above. Each later packet is signed over the RDATA, its own DNS payload, and the previous packet including its DNS header and SIG(0). Support of SIG(0) for TCP is OPTIONAL, and TSIG may be used instead, after setting up a key with TKEY if needed.

A message can have a single TSIG or one SIG(0), but not both.
sections.eli5: To make the seal you mix the message, and for an answer also the question, with a few details about the seal itself, then sign the whole mix. Change anything and the seal stops matching.

sections.title: Checking Signatures and Lifetime
sections.content:
A SIG record at the end of a response's additional section with type covered zero is a transaction signature for the response and its query. For TKEY responses it MUST be checked, and the message rejected if the checks fail, unless the TKEY mode says otherwise. For all other responses it MAY be checked and the message rejected on failure. Except to authenticate an update, TKEY or similar privileged request, servers are not required to check a request SIG(0).

A successful check does not directly prove that the data records are valid. It proves they were sent by the queried server and not altered. Only a proper SIG signed by the zone, or by a key tracing authority to it or to static resolver configuration, can authenticate data records directly. A resolver or server that does not implement these signatures MUST ignore them without error where they are optional, and treat them as failing where they are required.

The inception and expiration times resist replay attacks. They should form a time bracket outside which messages can be ignored, and in IP networks it should not normally extend more than 5 minutes into the past or into the future.
sections.eli5: A good seal shows the letter came from the right post office. It does not promise that what the letter says is true. Seals also carry a short expiry time so an old letter cannot be sent again.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content: The RFC adds no security considerations beyond those in RFC 2535. It does note that putting the SIG(0) inception and expiration times under the signature improves resistance to replay attacks. For IANA, no new parameters are created and no parameter values assigned.
sections.eli5: The only new safety trick is sealing the expiry time too, so nobody can replay an old message later.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2535
sections.content:
The appendix lists what changed from RFC 2535. Explanatory text on the differences between TSIG and SIG(0) is added. The signed data now includes the SIG(0) RDATA other than the signature itself, which secures the inception and expiration times. SIG(0) for TCP is specified.

Discussion of suitable inception and expiration times is added, along with wording that either a TSIG or one or more SIG(0)s may be present but not both. Some areas are reworded for clarity.
sections.eli5: This is the list of fixes: sealing the expiry time, explaining when to use which seal, and saying how it works over TCP.

cells: Secret keys installed at both requester and server
Public key stored in DNS as a KEY record; private key at the signer
Common to authenticate requests, and replies when the request was authenticated
Only when needed to show required privilege or identity

data.title: Signed data
data.code:
request:       data = RDATA | request - SIG(0)
response:      data = RDATA | full query | response - SIG(0)
TCP, later:    data = RDATA | DNS payload - SIG(0) | previous packet
